title: Thoracic Geometry and Exercise Hemodynamics in Symptomatic Mitral Valve Prolapse: Development and Internal Validation of a Three-Variable Nomogram
content: Background: Risk stratification remains challenging in symptomatic patients with mitral valve prolapse (MVP), preserved left ventricular (LV) systolic function, and non-severe mitral regurgitation (MR). Thoracic geometry and exercise-derived hemodynamics may provide complementary information on cardiovascular phenotype and clinical outcomes. This study investigated their associations with retrospectively documented cardiovascular events and developed an exploratory anatomical–functional nomogram. Methods: We included 140 symptomatic adults with MVP, LV ejection fraction ≥55%, and non-severe primary MR. Thoracic morphometry and exercise stress echocardiography were performed at the index assessment. Preceding non-fatal cardiovascular events requiring emergency or hospital-based care were retrospectively reconstructed. Cox regression was used to evaluate associations with historical event occurrence and develop a nomogram estimating 3- and 5-year event-free survival within the reconstructed observation period, with bootstrap internal validation. Results: Over a reconstructed observation period of 4.86 ± 4.62 years, 40 patients (28.6%) experienced at least one qualifying event: 4/58 (6.9%) with an antero-posterior (A-P) thoracic diameter < 13 cm versus 36/82 (43.9%) with a diameter ≥13 cm. Reduced thoracic depth was associated with smaller cardiac dimensions, less severe MR, and lower exercise-derived filling and pulmonary pressures, despite reduced exercise capacity and greater symptom burden. A-P diameter (hazard ratio [HR] per cm, 1.517; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.090–2.111; p = 0.013), peak-exercise E/e’ (HR per unit, 1.177; 95% CI, 1.024–1.352; p = 0.022), and peak-exercise systolic pulmonary artery pressure (HR per mmHg, 1.073; 95% CI, 1.005–1.145; p = 0.034) were independently associated with the reconstructed composite endpoint. The three-variable nomogram achieved an apparent Harrell's C-index of 0.804 and an optimism-corrected C-index of 0.791, although calibration deviations were observed. Conclusions: Integrating thoracic geometry with exercise-derived LV filling and pulmonary hemodynamics may improve cardiovascular phenotypic characterization in symptomatic MVP without severe MR. However, because predictor measurements followed the reconstructed events, the nomogram does not establish prospective predictive validity. Independent prospective external validation is required before clinical implementation.
